papers.what_it_is: arXiv preprint 2511.00964v1 (cs.LG, 2 Nov 2025) of the Machine Learning journal paper (journal per the team lead; page 1 of the PDF names no journal) that proves lower bounds on the true error of a fixed trained model using synthetic data plus a few labeled samples, and proposes the OSYN method.
papers.title_on_page_1: Using Synthetic Data to estimate the True Error is theoretically and practically doable
papers.venue_or_status_on_page_1: arXiv:2511.00964v1 [cs.LG] 2 Nov 2025 (preprint banner; no journal named on page 1)

assertions.value: Theorem 1 gives a high-probability LOWER bound on the true error F(P0,h) of one given trained model h: the synthetic-set error F(G,h) minus a local loss-sensitivity term minus a confidence term. The bound can be computed exactly once a synthetic set G exists and does not explicitly depend on the labeled sample size n. It bounds the error of a specific model h, not an irreducible (Bayes) error of the dataset; the paper never uses the term Bayes error. It holds with probability at least 1-delta1-delta2 under stated assumptions (model imperfect, F(G,h) at least eps_h+B, multinomial cell counts). The proof is in Appendix A (not independently verified here).
quotes: This theorem, which is proven in Appendix A, provides a lower bound for the true error of model h.
Last but not least, the lower bound (1) can be computed exactly, once we have G.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors prove it under explicit assumptions; the proof was not re-derived and the bound is for one model's error, not a dataset floor.

assertions.value: The authors state that OSYN rests only on a lower bound on a model's true error and has no upper bound, so it gives no two-sided confidence interval. (Theorem 2 gives an asymptotic upper-style bound, but OSYN as implemented uses the lower bound.) A lower bound says error is at least this high; it does not say whether error can still be reduced.
quotes: OSYN only relies on the lower bound on the true error of a model, but lack an upper bound to provide a two-sided confidence interval for the error estimate.
assertions.certainty_reason: Direct statement of the authors' own limitation.

assertions.value: In a Gaussian-mixture simulation with known P0 (oracle set much larger than the training set), the gap between oracle loss and the OSYN lower bound grew with the KL divergence of the generator from P0 across ten mean-shift scales for a Decision Tree. The Pearson correlation between gap and KL was 0.994. Measured on one model and one simulation family.
quotes: There is a strongly linear relationship between optimized gaps and KL values (Figure 1) with their Pearson correlation is 0.994.
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulation family and one classifier; correlation over ten points.

assertions.value: On CREDIT, BANK and ADULT tabular data, with a 500-row biased small test set drawn from a 70 percent oracle split and a CTGAN generator, OSYN lower bounds were often close to the oracle loss (mostly slightly below it), while bootstrap values from the small set were often above the oracle loss. The oracle loss is the model's loss on the held-out oracle split, not a Bayes floor. With a balanced test set the average OSYN gap fell from 0.0152 to 0.0083 across 8 models.
quotes: The obtained lower bounds estimated by OSYN are often close to the true loss for most models, similar to the results on the simulation data above.
most of the lower bounds produced by the bootstrap method are inaccurate, with values greater than the true loss.
assertions.certainty_reason: At least five runs per cell on three public datasets; the 'true loss' is a large held-out split.

assertions.value: OSYN depends critically on generator quality. The authors list failure when the synthetic distribution deviates substantially from the true data (loose bounds) and mode collapse that misses rare patterns. They recommend several hundred labeled samples and report no tests on high-dimensional or highly structured data. Rare-event data such as fraud is where mode collapse and a small labeled set are risks (reader's inference, not stated by the authors).
assertions.anchor: Section 6 failure modes and limitations, pp. 12-13 (approx.)
quotes: OSYN may fail if the synthetic distribution deviates substantially from the true data, leading to loose bounds.
we have not yet evaluated the method on high-dimensional or highly structured data, such as text or images
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own caveats; the fraud-specific implication is an inference.

methods.name: OSYN (optimized synthetic data lower bound on a trained model's true error)
methods.what_it_bounds: A high-probability lower bound on the true (test) error of one trained model h, tightened by choosing synthetic points near each labeled sample that maximize loss minus local loss difference.
methods.inputs_needed: Trained model h; a small labeled i.i.d. set S (several hundred recommended); a generator fitted to the data (CTGAN etc.); a partition into K cells (K near |S|); hyperparameters b and delta2.
methods.fails_when: Generator deviates substantially from the true distribution; mode collapse; labeled set tiny or very biased with a poor generator; high-dimensional or structured data untested; hyperparameters badly chosen (bound can land above the oracle loss and become invalid).
methods.quote: OSYN may fail if the synthetic distribution deviates substantially from the true data, leading to loose bounds.

papers.what_it_is: A Federal Reserve Board staff working paper presenting CardSim, a simulator of payment card transactions whose fraud flag comes from a naive Bayes ranking, with an ML demonstration on its output.
papers.title_on_page_1: CardSim: A Bayesian Simulator for Payment Card Fraud Detection Research
papers.venue_or_status_on_page_1: Finance and Economics Discussion Series 2025-017, Federal Reserve Board, February 2025 (staff working paper, preliminary materials)

assertions.value: The CardSim ground-truth label process is known and written down: five features (card type, location type, amount, distance, time) get marginal and fraud-conditional distributions, a naive Bayes posterior odds is computed per record, records are ranked by posterior odds, and the top p percent (default 1 percent) are labeled fraud. The label is therefore a deterministic rank cutoff of a known score. In principle that makes a true ceiling computable by applying the generator's own scoring function, but the paper does not compute one (reader's inference).
quotes: The final phase of the simulation leverages Bayes’ theorem to generate a ground truth fraud flag.
A one percent fraud ranking threshold guarantees that one percent of transactions will be labeled as fraud.
assertions.certainty_reason: The labeling mechanism is stated by the author; the ceiling consequence is flagged as inference.

assertions.value: The paper reports model performance on CardSim output but states no achievable maximum. Logistic regression, XGBoost and an MLP (chronological 70/30 split, 3.16 million records, 1 percent fraud) showed 76-81 percent precision and 57-65 percent recall, averaged over five runs, and XGBoost had the highest summary scores. The paper does not say how close these are to the best possible score under its own label process.
quotes: The candidate models display 76-81 percent precision and 57-65 percent recall.
Among the candidate models, the XGBoost has the highest overall summary scores, but its AUPRC is comparable to that of the neural network.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured means over five simulator runs; the absence of a ceiling is an observation about the paper, not a quotable claim.

assertions.value: CardSim fraud labels have no temporal or typology structure: payment class draws are independent events and a fraud flag does not affect later transactions. A ceiling computed on CardSim therefore cannot reflect sequence or recency signal that real card fraud may carry.
quotes: Payment class draws are independent events.
Whether or not a given payment is flagged as fraudulent has no effect on subsequent transactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author states it directly as a limitation.

assertions.value: Some CardSim fraud-process parameters are assumptions, not data: the modal quantile for fraudulent distance (0.75) is not empirically derived, and the author says some parameters have no real-world or theoretical basis. A ceiling computed on CardSim is a ceiling for an assumed process, not for real fraud.
quotes: fraudulent modal quantile is not empirically derived.
While the parameters selected in the simulator are chosen carefully and are meant to be plausible, some are not based on real world data or economic theory.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author's own caveats.

methods.name: Known generating process (naive Bayes posterior-odds rank labeling) as a ceiling device
methods.what_it_bounds: Would let one compute the exact best achievable score on the simulated data by applying the simulator's own scoring function; the paper does not do this.
methods.inputs_needed: Simulator parameters (marginals, conditionals, fraud multipliers, prior, rank threshold) and payer-specific amount averages.
methods.fails_when: The simulated process differs from real fraud (assumed parameters, independent draws, no typologies); the model lacks the payer-specific features the label depends on.
methods.quote: The final phase of the simulation leverages Bayes’ theorem to generate a ground truth fraud flag.

papers.what_it_is: NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks paper introducing AMLworld, an agent-based generator of synthetic multi-bank transactions with complete laundering labels, six public datasets, and GNN and gradient boosted tree baselines.
papers.title_on_page_1: Realistic Synthetic Financial Transactions for Anti-Money Laundering Models
papers.venue_or_status_on_page_1: arXiv:2306.16424v3 [cs.AI] 25 Jan 2024; NeurIPS 2023 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks

assertions.value: In AMLworld the generator knows the source of all illicit funds and tags them transitively through every later transaction, so every laundering transaction is labeled. The ground-truth label process is therefore known by construction. The paper does not compute a best-achievable score from it.
quotes: Since the generator knows the source of all funds, it knows which transfers are laundering.
AMLworld’s complete labeling of laundering is nearly impossible with real-world data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors as a design property; no ceiling analysis is given.

assertions.value: Best minority-class F1 on the six datasets (Table 2, p. 9) was 63.23 and 27.30 (HI-Small, LI-Small, GFP+XGBoost), 65.70 and 28.16 (HI-Medium, LI-Medium), 48.67 (HI-Large, GFP+LightGBM) and 24.23 (LI-Large, GFP+XGBoost). The authors attribute the harder LI sets to a lower illicit ratio and a longer pattern time span. They do not say whether the remaining gap is learnable from the features given. The table numbers come from the page text, not from the quotes.
quotes: The LI datasets present more significant predictive challenges compared to the HI datasets.
The primary difference between LI and HI datasets is that criminals launder less frequently in LI, which makes it harder to discover the laundering patterns.
assertions.certainty_reason: Means over seeds from the paper's own tables; the authors give no interpretation of the remaining gap.

assertions.value: The experiments exclude source and destination account IDs from the features so models cannot detect laundering by memorizing account IDs. If IDs were included, scores on this benchmark could be inflated and any ceiling estimate would be contaminated (reader's inference).
quotes: Source and destination account IDs of the transactions are not used as features in our experiments, which prevents our models from recognizing laundering transactions simply by learning account IDs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Direct statement of the experimental protocol; the inflation consequence is the reader's inference.

assertions.value: In the multi-bank experiments, sharing a model across banks raised F1 over private models, and sharing the transaction graph as well raised it further. This is evidence that information in the dataset (cross-bank visibility), not only model choice, sets achievable detection.
quotes: Figure 6 shows that, in general, financial institutions can achieve higher F1 scores by building shared machine learning models.
However, building shared models on top of shared financial transaction graphs leads to even more significant improvements.
assertions.certainty_reason: Per-bank results for the top 30 banks on synthetic data; the numbers are in a figure.

assertions.value: The authors warn that performance on the synthetic data might not translate one-to-one to real data, and that small parameter changes can shift aggregate results such as the laundering rate. A ceiling on these datasets is a ceiling for the simulated world.
quotes: they should bear in mind that performance might not translate one-to-one to real data.
minor parameter tweaks can sometimes yield significant changes in aggregate results, such as the laundering rate.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors state both caveats directly.

methods.name: Complete simulator-side labels (transitive illicit-fund tagging)
methods.what_it_bounds: Gives exact true labels for every transaction, which is the precondition for computing a true error floor; the paper does not compute that floor.
methods.inputs_needed: The generator state; the released public datasets carry the labels.
methods.fails_when: Simulated behavior differs from real laundering; label completeness is not realistic for real data; the generator code is not released, so the floor cannot be derived by re-running it.
methods.quote: Since the generator knows the source of all funds, it knows which transfers are laundering.

papers.what_it_is: Preprint presenting AMLGentex, an open-source agent-based generator and benchmark suite for anti-money-laundering data with tunable difficulty, label noise, and several experiments.
papers.title_on_page_1: AMLGENTEX: MOBILIZING DATA-DRIVEN RESEARCH TO COMBAT MONEY LAUNDERING
papers.venue_or_status_on_page_1: arXiv:2506.13989v2 [cs.SI] 25 Sep 2025 (no venue named on page 1)

assertions.value: AMLGentex ground-truth labels are known from the simulator: a node is labeled laundering if it appears in an injected laundering pattern within the window, even if it also makes legitimate transactions. Alert patterns are always injected. The paper does not compute a best-achievable score.
quotes: That is, a node is labeled as money laundering if it appears in a laundering pattern within window w, even if it also conducts legitimate transactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a formal definition by the authors.

assertions.value: AMLGentex tunes the laundering-behavior parameters by Bayesian optimization so that a decision tree reaches a target false positive rate (98 percent in the main dataset) and feature importances are made uniform. The authors call this a deliberate worst-case design. Low scores on these datasets therefore reflect chosen generator settings, not a natural ceiling.
assertions.anchor: Section 5 Hyperparameter tuning, pp. 7-8; Appendix F.1
quotes: To discourage reliance on single features, we define a second objective that promotes uniform Gini-based feature importance.
It represents a deliberate worst-case design choice, and AMLGENTEX allows users to modify, extend, or replace the objectives to align with their own goals.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors describe the design choice; the implication for ceilings is a direct reading.

assertions.value: AMLGentex can inject class noise and typology noise into the training graph with user-set flip probabilities, and can hide labels, so training labels can be decoupled from the known ground truth. This lets a user measure how label error limits performance against a known truth.
quotes: In AMLGENTEX, this labeling noise is managed by introducing two types of perturbations: class noise and typology noise.
These add controlled inaccuracies to the training graph, Gtrain, where the user sets a flip probability for both benign and illicit accounts.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors describe the mechanism; no quantitative noise-ceiling result is given.

assertions.value: On the 100,000-account dataset (1850 laundering accounts), performance (average precision at recall above 0.6) declined as the fraction of labeled nodes fell. Centralized training with 60 percent of labels gave average precision near 0.15, and the authors say the federated results leave substantial room for improvement. Results average 10 seeds on data deliberately tuned to be hard.
quotes: As shown in Fig. 7 (left), performance declines as label availability decreases, with models varying in sensitivity.
compared to the centralized setting, where accessing just 60% of the labels yields an average precision close to 0.15 the federated results suggest substantial room for improvement.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured on one tuned simulated dataset; the room for improvement is the authors' judgement, not a computed bound.

assertions.value: The authors state that data-free generated datasets should not be read as faithful replicas of production data; the suite is a research sandbox with explicit assumptions. Scores or ceilings on it do not carry over to real data.
quotes: the generated datasets should not be interpreted as faithful replicas of production data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Direct author caveat.

methods.name: Tunable simulator with known labels and injectable label noise
methods.what_it_bounds: Would allow a known-truth error floor to be set or computed by choosing generator parameters (for example the gap between normal and alert amount distributions); the paper does not compute a floor.
methods.inputs_needed: Generator parameters (degree distribution, typologies, amount distributions, noise flip probabilities).
methods.fails_when: Parameters are tuned toward an arbitrary FPR target, so difficulty is artificial; simulated data differs from real data.
methods.quote: It represents a deliberate worst-case design choice, and AMLGENTEX allows users to modify, extend, or replace the objectives to align with their own goals.

papers.what_it_is: A short empirical study of validation-selected combinatorial fusion of seven classifiers on the IEEE-CIS card fraud benchmark, plus a CTGAN augmentation negative result.
papers.title_on_page_1: Validation-Stage Combinatorial Fusion Analysis for Imbalanced Credit-Card Fraud Detection
papers.venue_or_status_on_page_1: arXiv:2606.10393v1 [cs.LG] 9 Jun 2026 (no venue named on page 1)

assertions.value: On IEEE-CIS (590,540 transactions, 3.50 percent fraud, stratified random 60/20/20 split), the best fusion of Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM beat the strongest single model (LightGBM) by 0.0062 AUC-ROC, 0.0219 AUPRC and 0.0280 F1; 1,000-resample bootstrap intervals excluded zero. Strong tuned boosting plus ensembling added only about two AUPRC points. This is an empirical measure of model-side headroom, not a ceiling.
assertions.anchor: Sections V.D and VI, Tables VI-VII, pp. 4-5
quotes: DEF WtScore improves over LightGBM by 0.0062 in AUC-ROC, 0.0219 in AUPRC, and 0.0280 in F1 (Table VI).
The gain is reliable but modest: about 0.6 percentage points in AUC-ROC and 2.2 points in AUPRC over LightGBM.
assertions.certainty_reason: One dataset, one random split, bootstrap over the test set only.

assertions.value: Best reported IEEE-CIS test scores in this study: AUC-ROC 0.9405, AUPRC 0.6699, F1 0.6373, from a stratified random split rather than a temporal one. A temporal split would likely score differently (reader's inference). These are achieved levels, not an upper bound.
quotes: The best configuration, DEF WtScore, reaches AUC-ROC = 0.9405, AUPRC = 0.6699, and F1 = 0.6373.
The split is stratified random rather than temporal, although TransactionDT would support time-based testing.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reported numbers from the paper; leakage-free per the authors, with the random split noted as a limitation.

assertions.value: Adding CTGAN synthetic fraud rows (trained on 12,398 training frauds, rebalanced to about balanced) lowered every retrained model and the best fusion (AUC-ROC down 0.0303, AUPRC down 0.0574, F1 down 0.0554). The authors say to read this narrowly (numeric treatment of high-cardinality fields). Synthetic data as a training aid did not help here.
quotes: In this configuration, augmentation hurts every retrained model and lowers CFA performance as well (Tables X and XI).
This result should be read narrowly.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single configuration; the authors caution it is not a claim that CTGAN can never help.

assertions.value: The fusion gain depended on the number of fraud examples. It matched or beat the best single model from a 1 percent training fraud ratio upward and underperformed at 0.5 percent. The authors attribute this (as a likely cause, not tested) to too few frauds to estimate diversity.
quotes: At 0.5%, it underperforms, likely because too few fraud examples are available to estimate RSC diversity reliably.
assertions.certainty_reason: The cause is the authors' hedged explanation; the effect comes from one ablation figure.

methods.name: Validation-selected ensemble gain over best single model (CFA) as a model-headroom probe
methods.what_it_bounds: Nothing absolute. It measures how much a combination of strong models beats the best single model on held-out data, an empirical lower estimate of remaining model-side headroom.
methods.inputs_needed: Several trained base classifiers, a validation set for subset and rule selection, a held-out test set, bootstrap resampling.
methods.fails_when: Too few positives to estimate diversity (0.5 percent ratio); base models highly correlated; random rather than temporal split; the gain says nothing about the data's irreducible error.
methods.quote: The gain is reliable but modest: about 0.6 percentage points in AUC-ROC and 2.2 points in AUPRC over LightGBM.

papers.what_it_is: An empirical preprint fitting error(N) = a*N^-b + c learning curves to 6 classical model families on 18 public tabular datasets, using runs from a 127-member graduate cohort.
papers.title_on_page_1: Scaling Laws for Classical Machine Learning on Tabular Data: An Empirical Benchmark Study
papers.venue_or_status_on_page_1: arXiv:2607.21866v2 [cs.LG] 28 Jul 2026; page 1 footer reads Preprint

assertions.value: The fitted c in error(N) = a*N^-b + c is called an irreducible-error floor, but it is estimated per (dataset, model) from seven training fractions with hyperparameters fixed across N. Median c on classification was 0.208 for Boosting (AUROC about 0.79), 0.110 for Random Forest and 0.139 for linear/logistic. Lasso's floor was essentially 1 because the model fails. So c is a floor for that model class and setup, and the paper says cells with c at or above the 0.15 target need a different model class.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.2, Table 3, p. 6; Section 4.5 p. 7; Section 6(i) p. 10
quotes: Lasso’s floor is essentially 1, reflecting the shrink-to-mean failure mode discussed above.
Fixed hyperparameters (no per-N tuning), so our b values are lower bounds for what proper model selection could achieve
assertions.certainty_reason: Fitted values from seven points per curve; the paper itself ties floors to model class and fixed hyperparameters.

assertions.value: Across 1,648 converged per-replicator fits, 77.7 percent reached R2 above 0.8 and 74.5 percent above 0.9. By family, 87.9 to 94.8 percent of tree ensemble, SVM and linear/logistic fits exceeded R2 0.8 (Boosting 92.4, Random Forest 87.9), but only 47.5 percent of Ridge and 23.8 percent of Lasso fits did. A high R2 on seven points does not by itself validate extrapolation to the floor (reader's inference).
quotes: Across all 1,648 converged per-replicator fits, 77.7% achieve R2 > 0.8 and 74.5% achieve R2 > 0.9
Ridge and especially Lasso fit poorly, with only 47.5% and 23.8% respectively above that threshold.
assertions.certainty_reason: Counts reported directly; the extrapolation caveat is the reader's inference.

assertions.value: Sample-size targets N* obtained by inverting the fit are flagged by the authors as statistically unreliable when they need extrapolation more than 10 times beyond the largest observed N; one linear-model cell implied about 2.8 billion rows. Some fits are degenerate (small a, c near 0). The largest dataset was 53,940 rows, and the authors say nothing about million-row settings.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.5 and Table 6 caption, pp. 7-8 and 13; Section 6(ii) p. 10
quotes: † marks N ⋆ requiring extrapolation more than 10× beyond the largest observed N for that dataset; these values are statistically unreliable and shown for completeness only.
we say nothing about million-row settings
assertions.certainty_reason: Direct author caveats on their own derived quantities.

assertions.value: With the random seed fixed, the exponent b varied across replicators by a mean coefficient of variation of 0.144 (unweighted over 71 cells with 5 or more replicators; 13 cells were byte-identical; size-weighted 0.131; 0.164 excluding byte-identical cells). 10 of 71 cells (14 percent) had CV at or above 0.30, which the authors say fits implementation bugs better than legitimate ambiguity. The authors attribute the spread to unconstrained protocol parts (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling) without isolating any one cause.
quotes: With the seed fixed this is not seed/sampling variance: it measures replicator-implementation spread induced by the unconstrained parts of the protocol (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling).
single-group scaling-law studies should report uncertainty intervals on b wide enough to accommodate this 14% floor
assertions.certainty_reason: Reported statistics are exact; the attribution to preprocessing is the author's description of unconstrained protocol parts, not a controlled test.

assertions.value: The author concludes that in tabular ML the floor c, not the exponent b, is the binding constraint, and that b alone is misleading for practical decisions. This is the author's interpretation of fits on 18 clean public datasets with default-style hyperparameters, not a theorem.
quotes: In tabular ML the floor, not the exponent, is the binding constraint.
The takeaway is that for practical decisions, b alone is misleading; what matters is the joint (b, c).
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' interpretation resting on fitted floors with the stated caveats.

methods.name: Learning-curve extrapolation: fit error(N) = a*N^-b + c by nonlinear least squares
methods.what_it_bounds: An estimated irreducible-error floor c for one model class and setup, plus the data needed (N*) to reach a target error.
methods.inputs_needed: Test error at several nested training sizes (here seven fractions 0.01 to 1.00), fixed hyperparameters, constraints on a, b (0 to 3) and c (0 to 1 for 1-AUROC).
methods.fails_when: Regularized linear models (Lasso shrinks to the mean so c is near 1; Ridge error can rise with N); extrapolation more than 10x beyond observed N; degenerate fits with c near 0; preprocessing and implementation choices move b by about 14 percent; the floor holds only for the fixed model class and hyperparameters.

facts.explanation: Supported pieces: the paper fits error(N) = a*N^-b + c per (dataset, model) and calls c the irreducible-error floor; tree ensembles fit cleanly (Boosting 92.4 percent and Random Forest 87.9 percent of fits with R2 above 0.8, so over 87 percent holds for both; across ALL families the figure is 77.7 percent); CV(b) = 0.144 with a fixed seed, about 14 percent movement in the exponent. Corrections: (1) c is a floor for that model class with fixed hyperparameters, estimated from seven points, not a dataset-level irreducible floor; Lasso's fitted floor is about 1 from model failure, and extrapolations beyond 10x are flagged unreliable. (2) The replicators were a graduate cohort of 127, each assigned 3 of 18 datasets (a partial, partially blocked replication, 11,536 runs), not 127 repeats of one setting. (3) The 0.144 is a mean over cells; the spread is attributed to unconstrained protocol parts (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling), and 14 percent of cells (CV at or above 0.30) are described as more consistent with implementation bugs. So 'preprocessing choices alone' overstates it. (4) The R2 above 0.8 range of 87.9 to 94.8 percent covers tree ensembles, SVM and linear/logistic together.
facts.quote: With the seed fixed this is not seed/sampling variance: it measures replicator-implementation spread induced by the unconstrained parts of the protocol (preprocessing, encoding, missing-value handling).
